name: Evolution by selection
rule: Anything with variation, selection and inheritance adapts without a designer.
plain: Wherever copies vary and some copies survive better, the survivors' traits spread. It happens to genes, ideas, companies and algorithms.

story.beat: The fungicide works: blight falls 95%. A month later it's back, and the fungicide barely touches it. Dox explains: the 5% that survived were the resistant ones, and they seeded the next generation. The colony selected for its own enemy. The new plan rotates two fungicides and never sprays at half strength.

examples.text: Stall designs that attract buyers get copied; the others vanish. The market 'evolves' without anyone designing it.
Jokes and rumours mutate as they're retold, and the most repeatable versions survive.
Ada's scheduling algorithm 'breeds' candidate schedules, keeps the best and mixes them. A genetic algorithm.

realCase.title: Antibiotic resistance
realCase.text: In his 1945 Nobel lecture, Alexander Fleming warned that underdosing penicillin would breed resistant bacteria. Decades of overuse in medicine and farming did exactly that. Drug-resistant infections are now a leading global health threat.
realCase.source: Alexander Fleming, Nobel Lecture (1945); WHO fact sheet on antimicrobial resistance

misuse: Treating evolution as 'progress' or as a moral rule ('survival of the fittest' as justification). It only means 'fits the current environment', which says nothing about what's good.
sources: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859)

predict.prompt: Fungicide kills 95% of blight. What happens after a month of daily use?
predict.why: The survivors were the resistant ones; they reproduce.

mcq.prompt: Which three conditions are needed for evolution?
mcq.why: Without any one of these, no adaptation.

whichModel.prompt: Spam filters block most spam; months later spam has changed to slip past them.
whichModel.why: Filters are selection pressure on spam variants.
